summary:
Echoes Beyond Earth treats the machines NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars as an
archaeological site that anyone can walk through. You spin a 3D globe of either world, pick a
lander, rover, helicopter or orbiter at its real coordinates, and open it up to see the 3D model,
the story of its mission and a small hands-on lab. You can throttle Ingenuity's rotors in air
about one percent as dense as ours, or try to keep Opportunity's solar panels alive through a
global dust storm. A voice companion lets each spacecraft tell its own story.
We built it for the "Abandoned but Not Forgotten" challenge. These missions ended long ago,
but what they found and what they paved the way for is still shaping exploration. The project
turns dry mission archives into something people can explore and remember.
details:
The app is built around two interactive globes, the Moon and Mars, drawn with reactglobe.gl. Nine pieces of NASA hardware sit on them at their documented positions. On the Moon these are the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage with its laser reflector and the Apollo 17 Challenger with its ALSEP station. On Mars they are Viking 1, Opportunity, Ingenuity and Mars Global Surveyor, which are the abandoned ones, plus Perseverance, MRO and MAVEN, which are still working and shown as future monuments. A filter switches between the abandoned set, which is the default view, and everything. Selecting an artifact opens a drawer on the right with an orbit-controllable 3D model built in Three.js, a breakdown of its main hardware, its story, its scientific results and a timeline. Each one also has a short interactive lab based on a real engineering problem. Examples are laser ranging from Earth to the Apollo 11 reflector, the Ingenuity rotor throttle, the Opportunity dust-storm slider, the Viking soil scoop and the Apollo 17 RTG power lab. When you finish with an artifact a short farewell sequence plays, and the app keeps count of which ones you have visited in the browser. A voice companion runs alongside all of this. It speaks as the spacecraft you are looking at and answers questions out loud, using Google Gemini with the NASA facts built into its instructions. If there is no API key or no connection, a set of prepared answers keeps it working. The app also has background space audio, sound effects, a mute button and a citations window listing the NASA sources. Our goals were to make mission archives approachable for students and the general public, to keep the human side of these missions from being forgotten, and to show how each generation of spacecraft built on the one before it. The app is built with React and Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS, uses Three.js for the models and react-globe.gl for the planets, and uses the browser's Web Speech API plus optional ElevenLabs voices for audio.
